caption:
Scite shows whether later papers supported or contrasted a study before you cite it.
Its Assistant answers research questions with linked sources, and Reference Check flags retracted papers in your draft.
The full step by step guide is on neurafeedai.com.

slides.headline: How to use *Scite AI* for a literature review

slides.heading: 1. Map the field with *Assistant*
paras: Ask a research question. Assistant answers with citations linked to real papers.
Table Mode lists each reference with its own answer, and Extract Data saves it as a CSV.

slides.heading: 2. Read the *Smart Citations*
paras: Every citing statement is tagged supporting, contrasting or mentioning, with the text around it.
Scite itself calls these signals, not quality scores.

slides.heading: 3. Filter out the *weak sources*
paras: Preprints are included by default. Open the settings to exclude them or rank by citations.
You can also limit results by date and publication type.

slides.heading: 4. Check every reference *yourself*
paras: Fact checks mark references verified or rejected, but librarians still found an unrelated paper cited.
Run Reference Check on your draft to catch retractions.

slides.hook: Follow for guides that save you hours on research, homework and work.

site_article.headline: How to use Scite AI for a literature review, step by step
site_article.dek: Scite shows how later papers cited a study, answers research questions with linked sources and checks your references for retractions. Here is how to use each part, what it costs and where it falls short.
site_article.summary: Scite is an AI research platform from Research Solutions that classifies citations as supporting, contrasting or mentioning. Its Assistant, Search, Collections and Reference Check cover most steps of a literature review, starting at $20 a month with a seven day trial for eligible new subscribers.
site_article.seo_title: How to use Scite AI for a literature review: step by step
site_article.seo_description: How to use Scite AI for a literature review: map a topic with Assistant, read Smart Citations, filter preprints, build Collections and check references.
site_article.answer_summary: Use Scite Assistant to map the topic and find key papers, read the Smart Citations to see whether later work supported or contrasted each finding, save papers in a Collection, and run Reference Check on your draft. Search other databases too, because Scite says its coverage is not exhaustive.

paragraphs.text: If you want to know how to use Scite AI for a literature review, start with what makes it different. Scite, now part of Research Solutions, reads the full text of papers and shows how later work cited each one. Every citation is labeled supporting, contrasting or mentioning, and you see the sentence around it. So you can tell whether a finding held up before you cite it.

Scite says it indexes more than 300 million papers with full text search. Its tools are Assistant for questions, Search, Reports on single papers, Collections for your library, Reference Check for drafts, a browser extension, a Zotero plugin and an MCP server that connects Scite to other AI chat apps.
Scite AI plans and the free trial

Scite's pricing page, updated on November 11, 2026, lists Basic at $20 a month or $144 a year, and Pro at $50 a month or $480 a year. Basic includes unlimited Assistant questions, full text search, Smart Citation Reports, citation alerts and Collections of up to 1,000 papers. Pro raises Collections to 10,000 papers and adds API access, patents, clinical trials and grants. New individual subscribers may be eligible for a seven day free trial on Basic or Pro, and you can cancel before it ends to avoid the first charge. Universities buy access through an Enterprise plan, so check your library first.
How to use Scite AI for a literature review

paragraphs.title: 1. Map the topic with Assistant
paragraphs.text: Open Scite Assistant and ask a plain research question. The answer is a short summary with citations linked to the papers it used. Scite's own tutorial suggests using this first pass to collect synonyms, theories, seminal papers, methods and open disputes, so your real searches use the right words.

paragraphs.title: Prompt 1: Map a research field
paragraphs.text: I am starting a literature review on [topic]. List the main theories, the most cited early papers, the common research methods and the questions where studies disagree. Cite the papers for each point.

paragraphs.title: 2. Tune the settings before you trust the list
paragraphs.text: Click the gear icon in Assistant. According to a review by HKU Libraries, you can change the model, the number of publications it consults, the date range and the publication type. Preprints are included by default, and they are not peer reviewed. In one HKU test, a third of the 28 sources were preprints. You can exclude them and rank results by citations instead of relevance.

paragraphs.title: 3. Switch to Table Mode for a source list
paragraphs.text: Table Mode puts each reference in a row with its own answer to your question. Extract Data then downloads the fields you pick as a CSV file. HKU Libraries also notes that since March 2026 you can paste a list of DOIs to get summaries, and since May 2026 you can upload a PDF or document and ask questions about it.

paragraphs.title: Prompt 2: Compare findings in a table
paragraphs.text: For studies published since [year] on [intervention] in [population], list the sample size, the method and the main result of each study. Note where results contradict each other.

paragraphs.title: 4. Read the Smart Citations on each key paper
paragraphs.text: Open a paper and look at its citation statements. Each one shows the citing sentence, the section of the citing paper it appears in and its label. On the paper page, Summarize gives a summary of the paper itself, and Summarize citations sums up what citing papers say about it. Scite's tutorial warns that a supporting citation does not prove a study is sound, and a contrasting one does not prove it is wrong.

paragraphs.title: 5. Search the full text, then keep a log
paragraphs.text: Use Scite Search with Boolean operators and exact phrases. Because it searches citation statements in the full text, it can find papers that discuss a method even when the title and abstract do not. Scite's tutorial says to record the database, the exact query, the filters, the date and the result count, and to run the same search in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science or your field's database.

paragraphs.title: 6. Save papers in a Collection
paragraphs.text: Build a Collection from search results, Assistant results, a Zotero or Mendeley import or a list of DOIs. Collections track new citations and alert you about retractions and editorial notices. Scite's tutorial suggests one main Collection plus smaller ones for each theme.

paragraphs.title: 7. Run Reference Check on your draft
paragraphs.text: When your draft and reference list are stable, upload the manuscript to Reference Check. It shows how each reference has been cited and flags retractions, editorial notices and contrasting evidence. Scite describes it as a safety net, not proof that your review is rigorous.

Install the browser extension. After you log in, it shows a badge with the counts of supporting, mentioning and contrasting citations next to papers you read online, and clicking it opens the paper's page in Scite.
Use Scite inside ChatGPT or Claude

Scite offers connectors for ChatGPT and Claude, and its MCP server also works with Copilot, Cursor and other MCP clients. In ChatGPT you type @Scite to ground a question in Scite's data. The pricing page says MCP access needs a paid plan, an active trial or an Enterprise license, and Basic includes 250 MCP credits a month.
Where Scite falls short

Coverage is the main limit. HKU Libraries points out that much scholarly content is still behind paywalls and that Scite's database is not exhaustive. Scite's own tutorial says it is not enough on its own for a systematic review. HKU also found an unrelated paper cited in an Assistant answer, and a result titled Untitled that still had a working DOI.
Scite is strongest at the step most AI tools skip: showing what other researchers said about a paper after it came out. Use it to find and vet sources, not as the only search behind your review.
Before you cite anything Assistant found, open the paper and confirm it says what the summary claims. HKU Libraries says the outputs should not be treated as definitive.
